# Graphit AST

AST is the indexed graph and source of a project: files, entities (functions, methods, types), their relationships (calls, references, implementations where indexed) and stored metrics. Use it first for code discovery, reading and structural analysis, because one graph query replaces many speculative file reads and gives anchors another agent can reuse. AST does not edit files, run builds or tests, or perform Git operations: use your native tools for those.

`project_dir` is a runtime MCP argument, not persisted project identity. In docs, Task, Memory and handoffs save project identity plus repository-relative paths; never copy a machine-specific checkout root. Resolve the local root again on each host. Stores follow the checked-out project version (Git branch; `main` without Git); optional `project_version` reaches another.

Persistence boundary for every module: shared project records hold only non-sensitive content the project needs (contracts, decisions, evidence, operations). Never persist personal or sensitive user/organization data, secrets, credentials, security-risk material, feelings or unconfirmed speculation. A durable, useful personal preference or correction belongs only in private user memory. Label technical hypotheses as hypotheses.

## Tools

| Need | Tool |
| --- | --- |
| Read a known file, a slice or one entity | `catalog_s_g__ast_source` |
| Find code by name or concept | `catalog_s_g__ast_search` |
| Learn the graph's labels, properties and edges | `catalog_s_g__ast_schema`, then `catalog_s_g__ast_sample` for example nodes and edges |
| Definitions, callers, metrics, impact | `catalog_s_g__ast_query` (readonly Cypher) |
| Page the neighbors of one exact node | `catalog_s_g__ast_neighborhood` |
| Installed code contexts (`id@version`) | `catalog_s_g__ast_imports` |
| Index health or an explicit rescan | `catalog_s_g__index_status`, `catalog_s_g__index_run` |
| Export a graph package (only when requested) | `catalog_s_g__ast_export` |

## Translate the local operation

| Intent / familiar local equivalent | Graphit operation |
| --- | --- |
| Search code: Grep, rg, grep, search_text, workspace search | Unknown file: `catalog_s_g__ast_search`, then verify selected hits with `catalog_s_g__ast_source`. Known file: source with pattern and context. |
| Locate a file: Glob, find, file search | `catalog_s_g__ast_schema` once, then `catalog_s_g__ast_query` on the advertised file/path property with a prefix/suffix/substring filter. This queries indexed files, not arbitrary filesystem globs. |
| Read code: Read, read_file, cat, open_file | `catalog_s_g__ast_source` with a returned relative path; select an entity or line range instead of dumping a file. |
| First/last lines: head, tail; excerpts: sed, line-range reads | Source head, tail, or start_line/end_line. There is no top parameter; k belongs to Root search. |
| Go to definition / document symbols / symbol search | Query the schema's entity label by name and path; use uid when available to disambiguate, then read source. |
| Find callers / call hierarchy / find usages | Query incoming/outgoing CALLS. REFERENCES and field-access edges answer only the relationships their schema actually indexes. |
| Complexity / impact analysis | Query cyclomatic_complexity; traverse callers at bounded depth; inspect affected source and tests before editing. |
| Go to implementation / type hierarchy | Inspect the schema for supported relationships first. If absent, inspect candidate types/method signatures and report the evidence limit; do not invent an edge. |

Choose the row for the question, not every row. After AST has located current-project code, focused local reads for patching are appropriate; do not repeat broad native discovery already answered by AST.

## Target and cheapest useful read

Cluster neighbors are Graphit-managed: use the returned `checkouts[].dir` as `project_dir` on AST search/source/schema/query, with paths relative to that target. Never switch to native grep/Glob/walks because it is outside cwd. Read the target AST skill/overrides; cache schema/evidence per target. Resolve unknown projects through Hub's cluster-first route. Only an installed artifact without checkout uses `context: id@version` without `project_dir`; never replace a known local path. `catalog_s_g__ast_imports` lists installed contexts. Read other-project/imported source through AST.

Known file → source directly. Unknown location → search with a focused query and `k: 5`: `fts` for identifier/text clues, `hybrid` for concepts. FTS is ranked indexed retrieval, not exact identifier equality or exhaustive repository regex. Verify hits in source; use a node query for exact names. Do not automatically pair search and query when one answers.

Before the first query for a target, call `catalog_s_g__ast_schema` and reuse it; `catalog_s_g__ast_sample` shows real example nodes and edges when property values are unclear. Labels, properties and edge directions come from that schema. Return only needed columns; use observed paths/UIDs, not guessed absolute-path matches. Structured tools, including schema, accept top-level strict boolean `ai_optimized`: omitted/`true` returns TOON text without duplicate JSON `structuredContent`; `false` selects JSON for machine consumers. Root AST Source retains its original text. Use a small `LIMIT` for investigation. A capped result never proves absence.

## Source recipes: search, head/tail, slices and entities

Examples are illustrative, not language, framework, layout or test-runner requirements. Adapt paths, symbols and test conventions to the project's languages and schema. For language-specific semantics, inspect its toolchain and authoritative public docs; Hub is not a prerequisite for public technology. These are MCP payloads, not shell commands; keep target fields consistent.

Unknown location — `catalog_s_g__ast_search`:
```json
{"project_dir":"/work/app","query":"ParseOrder","mode":"fts","k":5,"ai_optimized":true}
```

Known-file grep with surrounding evidence — `catalog_s_g__ast_source`:
```json
{"project_dir":"/work/app","path":"src/orders.go","pattern":"return err","before":3,"after":4,"line_numbers":true}
```

Literal `pattern` is a case-insensitive substring. `regex: true` uses the Rust `regex` crate's syntax (add `(?i)` if needed); this is not shell grep syntax. Match output includes original file line numbers and merges overlapping context. It searches only the selected file/span, not the repository.

For the same source call, replace the pattern/context fields with ONE of these selectors:

| Need | Selector fields |
| --- | --- |
| First 30 lines / last 30 lines | `"head":30` / `"tail":30` |
| File lines 40–85 inclusive | `"start_line":40,"end_line":85,"line_numbers":true` |
| One function and its branches | `"entity":"ParseOrder","entity_type":"Function","line_numbers":true` |
| Regex alternatives with context | `"pattern":"TODO|FIXME","regex":true,"before":2,"after":2` |

Selectors compose in this order: entity → range → head → tail → pattern. With `entity`, line ranges are relative to the entity, starting at 1; without it, they are file-relative. Use combinations only deliberately (head plus tail selects the tail of that head slice). For homonymous methods in one file, `entity_type` does not distinguish receivers: query their identities/line ranges and select the right one with `entity_key` (`{type:"string"|"int64",value}`) or a file range. Missing source may mean `ast.index_source` is disabled, not that the file is empty.

## Query recipes: definitions, callers, metrics and impact

Examples use labels/properties only if present in your target schema. `Function` may need to become `Method` or another observed label. After resolving a symbol, reuse its UID or its unambiguous path/name in every relationship query. Run each Cypher statement as the `query` of `catalog_s_g__ast_query` with the same target and `ai_optimized: true`.

File lookup (Glob-like suffix selection, not a glob expression):
```cypher
MATCH (f:File) WHERE f.relative_path ENDS WITH 'orders.go'
RETURN f.relative_path LIMIT 10
```

Definition, source interval and stored cyclomatic complexity:
```cypher
MATCH (f:Function) WHERE f.name = 'ParseOrder' AND f.path = 'src/orders.go'
RETURN f.uid, f.name, f.path, f.line_number, f.end_line, f.cyclomatic_complexity LIMIT 5
```

Missing, zero or unsupported metrics are not proof of trivial code; do not invent a complexity value. A score helps choose review/test focus, not a blanket rewrite threshold.

Direct callers (incoming call hierarchy) — complete MCP payload:
```json
{"project_dir":"/work/app","query":"MATCH (caller)-[:CALLS]->(f:Function) WHERE f.name = 'ParseOrder' AND f.path = 'src/orders.go' RETURN DISTINCT caller.name, caller.path LIMIT 10","ai_optimized":true}
```

Direct callees (outgoing dependencies):
```cypher
MATCH (f:Function)-[:CALLS]->(callee)
WHERE f.name = 'ParseOrder' AND f.path = 'src/orders.go'
RETURN DISTINCT callee.name, callee.path LIMIT 10
```

Potential impact up to two caller hops:
```cypher
MATCH (dependent)-[:CALLS*1..2]->(f:Function)
WHERE f.name = 'ParseOrder' AND f.path = 'src/orders.go'
RETURN DISTINCT dependent.name, dependent.path LIMIT 20
```

A reachability result is potential impact, not proof that every caller must change. Closed bounds such as `*1..2` are intentional: bare `*2` is not an exact two-hop bound in this planner. Expand depth only to resolve a concrete remaining risk.

Test candidates: add a reached-endpoint filter to the direct-caller query, e.g. `AND caller.path ENDS WITH '_test.go'` for Go. Tests may call through helpers, interfaces or runtime dispatch, so also inspect bounded indirect callers and known suites. A matching filename or empty direct-call result does not establish test coverage.

Relationship-query constraints: use `RETURN DISTINCT` and project properties of one endpoint only (as above). Put anchor and reached-node filters in separate top-level `AND` clauses; do not combine both endpoints inside one grouped predicate or cross-endpoint `OR`. For ordering, project the property/alias being sorted. Do not assume a general Cypher engine accepts `collect()`, `label()` or both-endpoint projections here; query the other endpoint separately, or page one node's neighbors with `catalog_s_g__ast_neighborhood`.

Neighborhood paging: `catalog_s_g__ast_neighborhood` takes the anchor's `anchor_label`, its typed primary key `anchor_key` (`{type:"string"|"int64",value}`) and `limit` (1–1000); optional `relationship`, `other_label` and `direction` (`incoming` or `outgoing`) filter the page, and omitting them returns both directions and all relationship families. Continue with the returned opaque `cursor`.

Implementations / type hierarchy: for a target whose schema advertises `(Class)-[:IMPLEMENTS]->(Interface)`, use its observed contract name/path:
```cypher
MATCH (impl:Class)-[:IMPLEMENTS]->(contract:Interface)
WHERE contract.name = 'OrderStore' AND contract.path = 'src/contracts.ts'
RETURN DISTINCT impl.name, impl.path LIMIT 10
```

Go interfaces are satisfied implicitly; do not expect an explicit `implements` declaration. If the target has no relevant edge, compare candidate type/method source with the interface and distinguish candidates from verified implementations. Treat `REFERENCES` according to its declared source/target kinds, not as universal find-usages. Unresolved stubs, empty source paths and dynamic dispatch limit graph completeness; no rows means only no indexed match.

## Integrated change workflow

Before writing an impact assessment, reconciling code with a documented contract, or handing an investigation to another agent, read [the completed impact case](references/impact-assessment.md). Simple lookups use the recipes above. If the local resource is unavailable, call `catalog_s_g__module_skill` with `module: ast`, `reference: references/impact-assessment.md` and the known `project_dir` when available.

For a request such as changing order validation: locate the definition → read relevant branches → inspect callers and test candidates → record affected contracts, files, dependencies and acceptance checks in Task before implementation. Use Knowledge for contracts and AST for current behavior. At any new question during exploration, recall Memory facts/lessons or Task investigations/decisions before guessing. Load each additional skill immediately before its module is needed; do not preload every module.

In Task preserve logical project/context and revision, relative source paths/lines, symbol names, metrics/relationships, limits and next validation. Keep host-bound UIDs only in the live query; normalize their provenance to relative path and symbol before saving. Surface discrepancies between code and Knowledge, then reconcile affected documentation. Stop retrieval once the scoped question has enough evidence to answer, plan or validate.

## Recovery and maintenance

For a database-open failure retry once, then inspect `catalog_s_g__index_status` (AST graph/source, lexical and embedding phases) and report the limitation. For a schema rejection refresh the schema once and correct the query; an unsupported planner form calls for a simpler supported query. Indexing is automatic: the daemon indexes writes and the adapter stop hook requests an asynchronous rescan, so do not duplicate or wait for it. For an explicit administrative repair, `catalog_s_g__index_run` (optional `input.module: "ast"`) requests the existing supervisor's coalesced full-project rescan; acceptance is not completion, and optional `wait_ms` follows it for a bounded time. Do not reset a corpus to repair a read. Delegated transports without these controls report the gap to the coordinator.

Use native discovery only when the required MCP tool is unavailable or current-project text is unsupported/unindexed; state this fallback once and do not substitute the Graphit CLI. When a decision requires freshness, inspect the selected source and content fingerprint exposed by that operation. `catalog_s_g__sync` reconciles installed artifacts and agent files; it does not wait for index completion. `catalog_s_g__ast_export` writes an admitted graph to the `output` package file and is a maintenance action, used only when requested.

# Complete impact assessment

Read this when an investigation must become a decision, executable plan or handoff. Sections: scope and evidence; interpret the result; contract reconciliation; recovery. A single source lookup does not require this workflow.

## Case: changing the AST instruction templates

Request: “Understand `skill_templates(Module::Ast)`, its consumers and the impact of changing the AST instructions.”

This case uses the current Rust selection and rendering path in Graphit. It identifies real source and test targets without asserting a caller count, stored complexity or test execution. Re-query the current target before acting. Replace /work/graphit-code only in the live MCP payload with the current host's verified root. Never save that expansion in the analysis, docs or handoff; persist Graphit project identity, revision and repository-relative file/symbol references. For a globally installed artifact without a checkout, use its resolved context instead of project_dir.

The analysis task's scope is template selection, rendering and affected consumers. It does not authorize changing instructions. Reuse its known requirements and relevant Knowledge pages; record uncertain intent instead of deciding that the implementation is automatically the contract.

### 1. Establish identity and read the definition

Call catalog_s_g__ast_schema with {"project_dir":"/work/graphit-code"} once. Use only labels, properties and relationships returned by the actual schema. For a schema exposing Function and the selected source fields, run this orienting query with catalog_s_g__ast_query:

~~~json
{"project_dir":"/work/graphit-code","query":"MATCH (f:Function) WHERE f.name = 'skill_templates' AND f.path = 'crates/graphit-runtime/src/skill_instructions.rs' RETURN f.uid, f.path, f.line_number, f.end_line, f.cyclomatic_complexity LIMIT 5","ai_optimized":true}
~~~

Treat returned identities and metrics as live evidence, not values supplied by this example. If a metric is absent, report it unavailable. Read the selected definition with catalog_s_g__ast_source:

~~~json
{"project_dir":"/work/graphit-code","path":"crates/graphit-runtime/src/skill_instructions.rs","entity":"skill_templates","entity_type":"Function","line_numbers":true}
~~~

The `Module::Ast` arm selects `skills/ast/entry.md`, its description and the `references/impact-assessment.md` companion from the captured template set. The corresponding Markdown sources live under `templates/agent-instructions/skills/ast/`. A selection function's control flow does not establish the correctness of its instructions; a wording change can still break a tool route or misdirect an agent.

### 2. Trace consumers, then inspect their actual behavior

Use the advertised type/layout schemas when authoring artifacts; do not guess destinations.

# Graphit Knowledge

`project_dir` is a runtime MCP argument, not persisted project identity. In docs, Task, Memory and handoffs save project identity plus repository-relative paths; never copy a machine-specific checkout root. Resolve the local root again on each host. Stores follow the checked-out project version (Git branch; `main` without Git); optional `project_version` reaches another.

Persistence boundary for every module: shared project records hold only non-sensitive content the project needs (contracts, decisions, evidence, operations). Never persist personal or sensitive user/organization data, secrets, credentials, security-risk material, feelings or unconfirmed speculation. A durable, useful personal preference or correction belongs only in private user memory. Label technical hypotheses as hypotheses.

Structured MCP calls accept top-level `ai_optimized`: omitted/`true` selects TOON text without duplicate JSON `structuredContent`; `false` selects JSON for machine consumers. Knowledge Source is a structured envelope: its Markdown string is preserved, rather than treated as a raw-text tool exception.

Knowledge is the project's maintained documentation, authored as Markdown under DOCS_ROOT and indexed into a searchable wiki. It is organized by business domain and reader goal, and must stay usable by someone, or another project, without this conversation. Task owns executable specifications, plans and results; AST proves code behavior; Memory holds durable constraints. Documentation is treated as code: it changes in the same work unit as the behavior it describes, because a page that drifts from the code misleads every later reader, human or agent.

| Need | Tool |
| --- | --- |
| Read a known page or a line range of it | `catalog_s_g__wiki_source` |
| Find pages by topic | `catalog_s_g__knowledge_search` |
| Catalogue pages by kind, source prefix, staleness or metadata errors | `catalog_s_g__knowledge_list` |
| Check the published corpus for broken references, missing metadata, orphan, short or stale pages | `catalog_s_g__knowledge_lint` |
| Follow outgoing links or find pages that reference a record | `catalog_s_g__knowledge_references` |
| See which pages changed in recent synchronizations | `catalog_s_g__wiki_log` |
| ID for a new page | `catalog_s_g__knowledge_id` |
| Index health or an explicit rescan | `catalog_s_g__index_status`, `catalog_s_g__index_run` |
| Export as a package or Markdown/OKF/Obsidian directory (only when requested) | `catalog_s_g__knowledge_export` |

`catalog_s_g__knowledge_ask` answers a question through a separate completion provider; as an agent, read the pages directly instead unless the engineer asks for it.

When a task, session, memory or knowledge page relies on another record, explicitly send `references` with each target's `type` and `id`, plus `relation` (for example supports, implements, derived_from or relates_to). Resolve real IDs through the corresponding read tools; never invent them. Mentioning an ID in prose or making a Markdown link does not create a database relation. Send the complete intended explicit list on reference changes; omit it to preserve existing relations, and send [] to clear explicit relations. Structural task/session links remain managed by their existing fields. Qualify cross-project/user targets with `scope` and `scope_id`, and imported knowledge with `context`; use logical identities, never checkout paths.
Example write input: `references: [{"target": {"type": "memory", "id": "<verified memory ID>"}, "relation": "supports"}]`. The source is the record being written; do not repeat a source ID. Read its existing references before replacing the list so unrelated links survive.
Use `catalog_s_g__task_references` for outgoing/incoming Task or Session relations, and `catalog_s_g__knowledge_references` for outgoing document relations or incoming logical-target references in the admitted Knowledge corpus. Keep each origin PROJECT/version, target type/scope/context and independent direction cursor. A recorded foreign relation grants no target-content access. Use only operations advertised by the selected transport; report missing projection/repair capabilities instead of inventing a generic query or reconcile tool.

For Knowledge, declare the same typed references in the authoritative Markdown YAML frontmatter under `references`, as a list of objects with `target: {type: memory, id: <verified ID>, scope: project, scope_id: <project ID>}` and `relation: derived_from`. Indexing persists that metadata. Keep existing frontmatter and reference entries when editing; an explicit `references: []` clears authored relations. Ordinary wiki links remain a separate persisted wiki-link relationship.

Retrieval alone needs no reference. Before planning/reorganizing docs or reviewing domain coverage, read [documentation design](references/documentation-design.md). Before first substantive domain authoring, read [worked domain](references/worked-domain.md); adapt depth, not its stack/rules/file count. Narrow maintenance needs only the design reference's per-unit consistency section when guidance is missing. Reuse retained references. `DOCS_ROOT` means this project's `docs/` or its existing authoritative location.
If local reference files are unavailable, use `catalog_s_g__module_skill` with `module: knowledge`, `reference: references/documentation-design.md` or `references/worked-domain.md`, and the known `project_dir` when available; request only the needed reference.

Known slug: call `catalog_s_g__wiki_source` with its exact `slug`. The result includes the slug, title and original Markdown in `selection.source`. For a long page use `selectors` to read its original lines:

```json
{"slug":"alpha","selectors":{"head":20,"line_numbers":true}}
```

Otherwise locate candidates through `catalog_s_g__knowledge_search`. Pass the query in `search`. Use the returned slug to open a result. A preview contains a summary or a short excerpt:

```json
{"search":{"query":"deployment policy","mode":"fts","top_k":5,"page_size":2,"preview":true}}
```

Preserve the returned slug, PROJECT/version and source selection. Both tools accept `source: {kind: project_knowledge}` or `source: {kind: imported_knowledge, artifact: {id, version, context_alias?}}`. For each new Knowledge page you are authorized to create without an explicit
ID, call `catalog_s_g__knowledge_id` with
`{"path":"docs/guide.md"}`, using the actual relative page path. Receive the real ULID, then save it as YAML frontmatter `id`
together with the document. Do not invent an ID, leave an empty placeholder or
omit this step. If the tool or authoring permission is unavailable, report the
missing capability instead of pretending the page was created with an ID.
Preserve a supplied explicit ID; editing or indexing an existing page does not
regenerate it. A saved ID preserves identity across a rename.

External documents and sources without frontmatter can still be published with
an automatic deterministic ULID derived from their validated relative origin.
The same origin keeps that fallback on reindex; a rename changes it unless an
explicit ID is retained. Its time component is not a creation timestamp.
Neither the tool nor the indexer writes the page or grants authoring access;
the authorized author saves the returned ID. There is no CLI generator.

# Designing and maintaining domain documentation

Read before a documentation set or coverage review. Use the per-unit consistency section for focused maintenance. This is a decision process, not a mandatory directory scaffold.

## 1. Discover the domain before proposing pages

Locate the configured DOCS_ROOT and current navigation, page conventions, language, supported releases and authoritative owners. Read relevant Knowledge pages, retained Task intent/decisions and selected AST entrypoints, contracts and tests. Use bounded searches around the requested capability; inspect cross-domain callers when they change the contract. A source tree describes implementation layout, not automatically the reader's domain model.

Identify:
- Audiences and goals: end users, administrators, integrators, operators, maintainers; include only real audiences.
- Journeys: trigger, prerequisites, normal sequence, completion signal, alternate paths, errors and recovery.
- Business rules: actor/permission, conditions, invariants, limits, lifecycle and deliberate exclusions. Preserve exact user constraints.
- Boundaries: owning component, consumers, external dependencies, authoritative data, supported interface/version and operations.
- Evidence: page/source/test/decision supporting each claim; distinguish observed behavior, intended behavior, assumption and unresolved gap.

For a whole-system request, inventory its business domains and their interactions before drafting any overview. For a narrow change, map only its affected domain plus real dependents. Unknown facts do not justify invented defaults for retention, access, error semantics or compatibility. Resolve consequential gaps through sources or focused clarification; keep unrelated work moving.

## 2. Build a coverage map and choose placement

Save a compact map in the active Task or a maintained domain overview when that is useful to readers:

| Domain / actor / journey | Rule or contract | Current evidence | Page / section | Gap / next action |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A real capability and who needs it | Observable condition and outcome | Exact source path/symbol, existing page or requirement | Existing target or justified new location | Covered, stale, missing, partial, conflicts or explicitly deferred |

A filename, headings, keyword match or a passing generic lint check is not coverage. Map all relevant journey classes: primary, alternate, exception, recovery and operational constraints; explain deliberate exclusions rather than creating empty sections.

- Root/index: audience entry points and domain navigation, with scope/version and links to shared concepts.
- Domain overview (explanation): vocabulary and glossary, business purpose, boundaries, rules, journeys, dependencies and navigation.
- User guide (how-to, or a tutorial for a first-time journey): one reader goal or coherent journey, with prerequisites, steps, outcomes and recovery.
- Technical reference/design (reference and explanation): stable contracts, architecture, data/state, integration boundaries, trade-offs and provenance.
- Operational guide (how-to for operators): deployment/migration/recovery or diagnosis when an operator has a real distinct job.
- Decision record: a consequential architectural choice with its context, the decision, its status and consequences. Never delete one; mark it superseded and link its successor. Record the same decision in Memory so agents recall it.

A migration/rollback recipe must say what state changes, compatibility conditions, what can fail and when to stop. Do not invent monitoring names, retention periods or performance promises.

Retain facts that affect a reader's decision, not the conversation transcript. Maintaining docs prepares reusable knowledge but does not itself authorize publication. Distinguish artifact/source version from actual deployed behavior.

# Find, archive and restore projects

Use this guide to retrieve previous work or move a project out of the active queue without deleting its content. Applies to Workboard 2.4.

## Before you start

Sign in to the correct workspace. Readers may list/view projects; a maintainer role is required to archive or restore. Use a sandbox project if practicing: lifecycle changes affect everyone working on that project. Before archiving, tell collaborators through your normal process that new tasks will be blocked; the product does not send that notice for you.

## Find a project

1. Open Projects in the intended workspace. “Show archived” starts unchecked.
2. Look for the project by its name. The initial list contains only active projects you can read.
3. If it is missing, turn on “Show archived”. Archived entries appear with an Archived badge; unrelated workspaces remain invisible.
4. Open the project. Confirm its name, workspace and status before any change.

An empty list means no projects match your access and filter; it does not prove that a project was deleted. If it remains missing, use [operational diagnosis](../operations/resolve-lifecycle-problems.md#missing-project).

## Archive an active project

1. Open the project's details and confirm that it is Active.
2. As a maintainer, choose Archive and review the confirmation naming the project and explaining that new tasks will be blocked.
3. Confirm Archive once. Wait for the details page to show Archived.
4. Return to Projects with “Show archived” off: the project is absent. Turn it on: the same project appears with its existing tasks and membership.

Archiving preserves existing work; it does not grant or revoke access. Creating a new task now shows “Restore this project before adding tasks.” To resume work, restore the project instead of creating a duplicate.

## Restore an archived project

1. Find the project with “Show archived” enabled and open it.
2. As a maintainer, choose Restore.
3. Wait for Active. The project now appears with “Show archived” off and new task creation is available again.

The existing tasks are still there; restoration does not recreate or duplicate them.

## Problems and recovery

| What you see | Meaning | Next action |
|---|---|---|
| Archive/Restore unavailable to a reader | Your role cannot change lifecycle | Ask your workspace maintainer to perform the change or grant the appropriate role through the normal access process. |
| “Project changed; refresh before retrying” | Another action changed the project after you opened it | Refresh, read the current state, and decide whether your intended change still applies. Do not repeatedly click the stale action. |
| Request times out or connection drops | The server may have committed the change | Refresh details first. If already in the desired state, stop. If status is unclear, follow [conflict or timeout diagnosis](../operations/resolve-lifecycle-problems.md#conflict-or-timeout). |
| “Restore this project before adding tasks” | The project is archived | Restore as a maintainer, then create the task once. Do not retry creation indefinitely. |
| Project not found | Wrong workspace, missing access or unknown ID | Check workspace and filter; have an authorized maintainer verify access without exposing data from another workspace. |

For API integrations use the [technical contract](../reference/lifecycle.md); for business meaning use [Project lifecycle](../index.md).

# Project lifecycle contract

Audience: integrators and maintainers. Applies to Workboard API release 2.4, after database migration 024. This is the current contract for the illustrative release, not a proposed API. The browser and other consumers use the same authorization and lifecycle service.

## Architecture and ownership

The authenticated HTTP handler derives the subject/workspace, validates input and calls the project service. The service applies membership/role checks. list_projects applies access filtering before the status predicate. archive_project, restore_project and create_task serialize on the same project row so task creation cannot pass an earlier active check while an archive commits. Repository writes and lifecycle audit events share one database transaction.

Responsibilities and source provenance:
- src/projects/list.rs / list_projects: filtering and query defaults.
- src/projects/lifecycle.rs / archive_project, restore_project: access, revision checks and transitions.
- src/tasks/create.rs / create_task: archived-project guard under the project lock.
- src/projects/model.rs and migrations/024_project_archive.sql: authoritative row shape and constraints.
- web/projects/list.tsx, web/projects/detail.tsx: UI controls and state refresh; these are consumers, not authorization boundaries.
- src/projects/list.rs::tests, src/projects/lifecycle.rs::tests and tests/e2e/project_lifecycle.spec.ts: contract and user-journey verification.

Repository-relative references identify the release-2.4 source baseline in this example. In real documentation, record the actual release/commit inspected. A supported API is the integration boundary; importing these internal packages is not a supported alternative.

## Read and list

The caller must have project-read access in the authenticated workspace.

GET /projects?include_archived=true includes both states the caller may read. Omit the parameter or pass false to return active only. Only literal true/false are valid; any other nonempty value returns 400 invalid_include_archived. GET /projects/{id} returns one accessible project in either state.

Example response for GET /projects?include_archived=true:

~~~json
{
  "items": [
    {"id":"p-17","workspace_id":"w-3","name":"Launch","status":"archived","revision":8,
     "archived_at":"2026-08-10T14:00:00Z","archived_by":"u-9"}
  ]
}
~~~

No matching rows returns 200 with items: []; it does not reveal whether inaccessible projects exist. Filtering does not alter the shape or membership rules. This example's endpoint returns all matching rows; do not infer a pagination contract for a real service without verifying it.

## Mutations and retries

POST /projects/{id}/archive and POST /projects/{id}/restore require maintainer access and a JSON body containing the last observed revision:

~~~json
{"expected_revision":8}
~~~

A successful transition returns 200 with the updated project representation and revision. Archive records the authenticated actor and a UTC timestamp; restore clears those archive fields. If the current state already matches the requested state and expected_revision is current, return 200 with the unchanged representation and no new audit event.

Validate authorization before revealing state. Check expected_revision before the no-op decision: a stale request returns 409 revision_conflict even if another actor already reached the desired state. After conflict or an uncertain network result, GET the project, evaluate its state and retry only if a change is still intended, using the returned revision. Do not replay the old revision blindly.

## Data and transition invariants

| Field | Meaning / invariant |
|---|---|
| id | Immutable project identity; belongs to one workspace. |
| workspace_id | Immutable access boundary for this contract. |
| status | Exactly active or archived. |
| revision | Positive integer, incremented once per effective lifecycle transition. No-op leaves it unchanged. |
| archived_at / archived_by | Both absent for active; both present for archived. Timestamp in UTC; actor is server-derived. |

| Current state / operation | Result | Effects |
|---|---|---|
| active / archive, current revision, maintainer | archived | Increment revision; set archive fields; one project.archived event. |
| archived / restore, current revision, maintainer | active | Increment revision; clear archive fields; one project.restored event. |
| already desired state / same action, current revision | unchanged | No new event or revision. |
| either state / stale revision | unchanged | 409 revision_conflict. |
| archived / create task | unchanged | 409 project_archived; no task inserted. |

Archive does not move/delete tasks, change their IDs or modify membership. State, revision, archive fields and one audit event commit atomically; transaction failure exposes neither a partial transition nor a successful mutation response. Archive and task creation use the same lock: whichever commits first determines whether that creation is accepted. Existing tasks stay readable under ordinary permissions. No retention worker deletes them in release 2.4.

## Access and errors

| Condition | Response / guarantee |
|---|---|
| Unauthenticated | 401 unauthenticated. |
| Unknown or inaccessible project ID | 404 project_not_found; do not distinguish the cases. |
| Accessible project but caller is a reader performing a mutation | 403 maintainer_required. |
| Missing/non-positive/non-integer expected_revision | 400 invalid_revision. |
| Stale revision | 409 revision_conflict; caller must reread. |
| New task on archived project | 409 project_archived; no partial task. |

Errors use {"error":{"code":"revision_conflict","message":"Project changed; refresh before retrying"}} with the condition's code/message. Consumers branch on code, not localized message text. Permission and input errors are not transient retry signals.

## Version and operational boundaries

The default list excludes archived projects starting in 2.4. Consumers that previously depended on archived results must explicitly send include_archived=true. Deploy migration 024 before the 2.4 service; old binaries are not supported against lifecycle writes until their compatibility has been checked. This domain has no feature flag, archive TTL, bulk mutation or automatic retry policy. Do not invent one.

Use [operational diagnosis](../operations/resolve-lifecycle-problems.md) for uncertain outcomes. Use [the user guide](../guides/find-archive-restore.md) for UI workflows and [domain rules](../index.md) for business meaning. Change verification belongs in Task; this page records the supported contract and source baseline.

# Resolve lifecycle problems

Audience: support operators with read access; lifecycle changes additionally require maintainer access. Applies to Workboard 2.4. Diagnose the project in its intended workspace. Do not modify database rows or membership to bypass lifecycle/access checks.

## Missing project

1. Verify the signed-in workspace and whether “Show archived” is enabled.
2. If you know the project ID, use the authorized project details view or GET /projects/{id}.
3. An Archived response explains absence from the default list. A 404 cannot distinguish an unknown ID from missing access; use the normal access-verification process with an authorized maintainer.
4. Confirm recovery by locating the intended accessible project. Do not restore solely to make it visible; readers can enable “Show archived”.

## Conflict or timeout

Capture the project ID, workspace, approximate request time and request correlation ID if returned. Do not capture access tokens.

1. Reread GET /projects/{id} with the same authorized workspace identity.
2. Compare the returned status/revision with the desired action. If already achieved, stop; a retry is unnecessary.
3. If investigation is needed, an authorized operator inspects the corresponding project.archived/project.restored audit event in the existing audit console. Its project, actor, timestamp and revision identify the transition; repeated identical-state requests should have no extra event.
4. If still in the other state, confirm the action is still wanted and use the latest revision once. Repeated conflicts require coordinating competing changes, not an unbounded retry loop.
5. A failed diagnostic read means outcome remains unknown. Record that limitation and escalate with the captured identifiers; do not report that archive failed merely because the network failed.

Recovery is verified when the authorized read shows the intended state and ordinary list/task behavior matches that state.

## Task creation blocked

Read project status. If archived, a maintainer must restore before a task can be created. If active, capture the observed revision/error and investigate concurrent lifecycle activity. After restoration, retry creation using the application's normal duplicate-prevention rules; this lifecycle contract does not define a task-creation idempotency key.

## Release or database mismatch

Check service release and the migration-024 record through the standard deployment tooling. Stop lifecycle writes and escalate if rollout order or compatibility is uncertain. Do not roll back by removing archive metadata or manually clearing status. A data rollback procedure is not defined by this release's lifecycle contract; use the verified deployment recovery procedure for the actual environment.

[Technical guarantees](../reference/lifecycle.md) · [User steps](../guides/find-archive-restore.md) · [Domain overview](../index.md).

# Find, archive and restore projects

Use this guide to retrieve previous work or move a project out of the active queue without deleting its content. Applies to Workboard 2.4.

## Before you start

Sign in to the correct workspace. Readers may list/view projects; a maintainer role is required to archive or restore. Use a sandbox project if practicing: lifecycle changes affect everyone working on that project. Before archiving, tell collaborators through your normal process that new tasks will be blocked; the product does not send that notice for you.

## Find a project

1. Open Projects in the intended workspace. “Show archived” starts unchecked.
2. Look for the project by its name. The initial list contains only active projects you can read.
3. If it is missing, turn on “Show archived”. Archived entries appear with an Archived badge; unrelated workspaces remain invisible.
4. Open the project. Confirm its name, workspace and status before any change.

An empty list means no projects match your access and filter; it does not prove that a project was deleted. If it remains missing, use [operational diagnosis](../operations/resolve-lifecycle-problems.md#missing-project).

## Archive an active project

1. Open the project's details and confirm that it is Active.
2. As a maintainer, choose Archive and review the confirmation naming the project and explaining that new tasks will be blocked.
3. Confirm Archive once. Wait for the details page to show Archived.
4. Return to Projects with “Show archived” off: the project is absent. Turn it on: the same project appears with its existing tasks and membership.

Archiving preserves existing work; it does not grant or revoke access. Creating a new task now shows “Restore this project before adding tasks.” To resume work, restore the project instead of creating a duplicate.

## Restore an archived project

1. Find the project with “Show archived” enabled and open it.
2. As a maintainer, choose Restore.
3. Wait for Active. The project now appears with “Show archived” off and new task creation is available again.

The existing tasks are still there; restoration does not recreate or duplicate them.

## Problems and recovery

| What you see | Meaning | Next action |
|---|---|---|
| Archive/Restore unavailable to a reader | Your role cannot change lifecycle | Ask your workspace maintainer to perform the change or grant the appropriate role through the normal access process. |
| “Project changed; refresh before retrying” | Another action changed the project after you opened it | Refresh, read the current state, and decide whether your intended change still applies. Do not repeatedly click the stale action. |
| Request times out or connection drops | The server may have committed the change | Refresh details first. If already in the desired state, stop. If status is unclear, follow [conflict or timeout diagnosis](../operations/resolve-lifecycle-problems.md#conflict-or-timeout). |
| “Restore this project before adding tasks” | The project is archived | Restore as a maintainer, then create the task once. Do not retry creation indefinitely. |
| Project not found | Wrong workspace, missing access or unknown ID | Check workspace and filter; have an authorized maintainer verify access without exposing data from another workspace. |

For API integrations use the [technical contract](../reference/lifecycle.md); for business meaning use [Project lifecycle](../index.md).

# Project lifecycle contract

Audience: integrators and maintainers. Applies to Workboard API release 2.4, after database migration 024. This is the current contract for the illustrative release, not a proposed API. The browser and other consumers use the same authorization and lifecycle service.

## Architecture and ownership

The authenticated HTTP handler derives the subject/workspace, validates input and calls the project service. The service applies membership/role checks. list_projects applies access filtering before the status predicate. archive_project, restore_project and create_task serialize on the same project row so task creation cannot pass an earlier active check while an archive commits. Repository writes and lifecycle audit events share one database transaction.

Responsibilities and source provenance:
- src/projects/list.rs / list_projects: filtering and query defaults.
- src/projects/lifecycle.rs / archive_project, restore_project: access, revision checks and transitions.
- src/tasks/create.rs / create_task: archived-project guard under the project lock.
- src/projects/model.rs and migrations/024_project_archive.sql: authoritative row shape and constraints.
- web/projects/list.tsx, web/projects/detail.tsx: UI controls and state refresh; these are consumers, not authorization boundaries.
- src/projects/list.rs::tests, src/projects/lifecycle.rs::tests and tests/e2e/project_lifecycle.spec.ts: contract and user-journey verification.

Repository-relative references identify the release-2.4 source baseline in this example. In real documentation, record the actual release/commit inspected. A supported API is the integration boundary; importing these internal packages is not a supported alternative.

## Read and list

The caller must have project-read access in the authenticated workspace.

GET /projects?include_archived=true includes both states the caller may read. Omit the parameter or pass false to return active only. Only literal true/false are valid; any other nonempty value returns 400 invalid_include_archived. GET /projects/{id} returns one accessible project in either state.

Example response for GET /projects?include_archived=true:

~~~json
{
  "items": [
    {"id":"p-17","workspace_id":"w-3","name":"Launch","status":"archived","revision":8,
     "archived_at":"2026-08-10T14:00:00Z","archived_by":"u-9"}
  ]
}
~~~

No matching rows returns 200 with items: []; it does not reveal whether inaccessible projects exist. Filtering does not alter the shape or membership rules. This example's endpoint returns all matching rows; do not infer a pagination contract for a real service without verifying it.

## Mutations and retries

POST /projects/{id}/archive and POST /projects/{id}/restore require maintainer access and a JSON body containing the last observed revision:

~~~json
{"expected_revision":8}
~~~

A successful transition returns 200 with the updated project representation and revision. Archive records the authenticated actor and a UTC timestamp; restore clears those archive fields. If the current state already matches the requested state and expected_revision is current, return 200 with the unchanged representation and no new audit event.

Validate authorization before revealing state. Check expected_revision before the no-op decision: a stale request returns 409 revision_conflict even if another actor already reached the desired state. After conflict or an uncertain network result, GET the project, evaluate its state and retry only if a change is still intended, using the returned revision. Do not replay the old revision blindly.

## Data and transition invariants

| Field | Meaning / invariant |
|---|---|
| id | Immutable project identity; belongs to one workspace. |
| workspace_id | Immutable access boundary for this contract. |
| status | Exactly active or archived. |
| revision | Positive integer, incremented once per effective lifecycle transition. No-op leaves it unchanged. |
| archived_at / archived_by | Both absent for active; both present for archived. Timestamp in UTC; actor is server-derived. |

| Current state / operation | Result | Effects |
|---|---|---|
| active / archive, current revision, maintainer | archived | Increment revision; set archive fields; one project.archived event. |
| archived / restore, current revision, maintainer | active | Increment revision; clear archive fields; one project.restored event. |
| already desired state / same action, current revision | unchanged | No new event or revision. |
| either state / stale revision | unchanged | 409 revision_conflict. |
| archived / create task | unchanged | 409 project_archived; no task inserted. |

Archive does not move/delete tasks, change their IDs or modify membership. State, revision, archive fields and one audit event commit atomically; transaction failure exposes neither a partial transition nor a successful mutation response. Archive and task creation use the same lock: whichever commits first determines whether that creation is accepted. Existing tasks stay readable under ordinary permissions. No retention worker deletes them in release 2.4.

## Access and errors

| Condition | Response / guarantee |
|---|---|
| Unauthenticated | 401 unauthenticated. |
| Unknown or inaccessible project ID | 404 project_not_found; do not distinguish the cases. |
| Accessible project but caller is a reader performing a mutation | 403 maintainer_required. |
| Missing/non-positive/non-integer expected_revision | 400 invalid_revision. |
| Stale revision | 409 revision_conflict; caller must reread. |
| New task on archived project | 409 project_archived; no partial task. |

Errors use {"error":{"code":"revision_conflict","message":"Project changed; refresh before retrying"}} with the condition's code/message. Consumers branch on code, not localized message text. Permission and input errors are not transient retry signals.

## Version and operational boundaries

The default list excludes archived projects starting in 2.4. Consumers that previously depended on archived results must explicitly send include_archived=true. Deploy migration 024 before the 2.4 service; old binaries are not supported against lifecycle writes until their compatibility has been checked. This domain has no feature flag, archive TTL, bulk mutation or automatic retry policy. Do not invent one.

Use [operational diagnosis](../operations/resolve-lifecycle-problems.md) for uncertain outcomes. Use [the user guide](../guides/find-archive-restore.md) for UI workflows and [domain rules](../index.md) for business meaning. Change verification belongs in Task; this page records the supported contract and source baseline.

# Resolve lifecycle problems

Audience: support operators with read access; lifecycle changes additionally require maintainer access. Applies to Workboard 2.4. Diagnose the project in its intended workspace. Do not modify database rows or membership to bypass lifecycle/access checks.

## Missing project

1. Verify the signed-in workspace and whether “Show archived” is enabled.
2. If you know the project ID, use the authorized project details view or GET /projects/{id}.
3. An Archived response explains absence from the default list. A 404 cannot distinguish an unknown ID from missing access; use the normal access-verification process with an authorized maintainer.
4. Confirm recovery by locating the intended accessible project. Do not restore solely to make it visible; readers can enable “Show archived”.

## Conflict or timeout

Capture the project ID, workspace, approximate request time and request correlation ID if returned. Do not capture access tokens.

1. Reread GET /projects/{id} with the same authorized workspace identity.
2. Compare the returned status/revision with the desired action. If already achieved, stop; a retry is unnecessary.
3. If investigation is needed, an authorized operator inspects the corresponding project.archived/project.restored audit event in the existing audit console. Its project, actor, timestamp and revision identify the transition; repeated identical-state requests should have no extra event.
4. If still in the other state, confirm the action is still wanted and use the latest revision once. Repeated conflicts require coordinating competing changes, not an unbounded retry loop.
5. A failed diagnostic read means outcome remains unknown. Record that limitation and escalate with the captured identifiers; do not report that archive failed merely because the network failed.

Recovery is verified when the authorized read shows the intended state and ordinary list/task behavior matches that state.

## Task creation blocked

Read project status. If archived, a maintainer must restore before a task can be created. If active, capture the observed revision/error and investigate concurrent lifecycle activity. After restoration, retry creation using the application's normal duplicate-prevention rules; this lifecycle contract does not define a task-creation idempotency key.

## Release or database mismatch

Check service release and the migration-024 record through the standard deployment tooling. Stop lifecycle writes and escalate if rollout order or compatibility is uncertain. Do not roll back by removing archive metadata or manually clearing status. A data rollback procedure is not defined by this release's lifecycle contract; use the verified deployment recovery procedure for the actual environment.

[Technical guarantees](../reference/lifecycle.md) · [User steps](../guides/find-archive-restore.md) · [Domain overview](../index.md).
~~~~

Illustrative Task evidence packet (a real agent must replace it with observed results):
- Targets: src/projects/list.rs::list_projects, src/projects/list.rs::tests, list.tsx, all five page paths above; lifecycle.rs inspected for unchanged archive/restore semantics.
- Requirement coverage: R1/R2 → list_default, list_false, list_includes_archived, list_access_isolation → guide “Find a project” and contract “Read and list”.
- Validation to execute: cargo test --locked projects and the project's configured end-to-end runner for project_lifecycle.spec.ts. Default/off must show only accessible active records; on must add accessible archived records; neither shows inaccessible records. Do not substitute an invented test command.
- Documentation check: follow root→domain→guide→contract→runbook links and compare example IDs/status/revision; search affected pages for the obsolete all-states default.
- Record actual command exit/output, browser observations and failures in Task checks. If the browser runner is unavailable, the end-to-end check is pending; source agreement alone does not prove the UI scenario passed.

## Drift exercise B: docs → code without manufacturing a feature

Fixture request: improve the archive guide. An existing draft says “Archived projects are deleted after 30 days.” AST inspection of lifecycle.rs, model.rs, migration 024 and the configured job entrypoints finds archive/restore state only; no timer, deletion job or accepted retention requirement supports that sentence.

Classify the statement as unsupported current-behavior documentation, not an invitation to add a retention worker. Check the release contract and Task intent. In this fixture both confirm preservation until an explicit lifecycle change. Correct the guide/domain overview to state that release 2.4 has no automatic deletion; keep the actual retention policy outside this bounded contract unless authoritative evidence defines one. Verify the archive/restore and preservation tests and affected links; record inspected sources and actual results.

If the user instead explicitly requests a future 30-day retention policy, preserve it as proposed intent in a clearly labeled specification with unresolved requirements (start time, exemptions, permissions, recovery and migration). Link a Task planning unit. Do not present a runnable deletion API, promise recoverability, mark delivery checks passed or implement it from a docs-only request.

Illustrative completed-unit evidence distinguishes the two:
- Documentation correction: unsupported claim removed; source/test targets named; user/technical pages agree about the current release. No code change needed, because no accepted current requirement was violated.
- Future design alternative: intent documented, implementation missing, planning Task open; current user guide still states actual behavior. The documentation/design unit may complete on its own checks; the future feature is not implemented.

## Cold-reader review of the set

A reader can find archived work and recover from a missing project without knowing database internals. A maintainer can predict preservation and the new-task restriction. An integrator can construct requests, interpret defaults/errors and retry against a current revision without internal-package access. An operator can diagnose uncertain outcomes without guessing success or editing storage.

Review the real delivered set using those scenarios, not by counting files or checking that headings exist. Search and source-read selected pages after indexing only when retrieval/navigation freshness needs verification; do not force a full sync after every documentation edit. Publishing these pages through Hub is a separate authorized action with verified artifact/version/target.

# Graphit Memory

Memory holds what future work in this project needs to know and cannot cheaply rediscover: confirmed decisions with their reasons, conventions, corrections and lessons. Task holds current progress and evidence; Knowledge holds maintained documentation. Read [recall and decided persistence cases](references/durable-context.md) when a new question, correction or durable finding needs guidance, and reuse it afterward.

Persistence boundary for every module: shared project records hold only non-sensitive content the project needs (contracts, decisions, evidence, operations). Never persist personal or sensitive user/organization data, secrets, credentials, security-risk material, feelings or unconfirmed speculation. A durable, useful personal preference or correction belongs only in private user memory. Label technical hypotheses as hypotheses.

## Recall

Mandatory Memory arrives through the session hook: treat it as standing context and do not fetch it again. Recall again whenever a new doubt appears about the system, a rationale or learned behavior, at any point in the work and not only at session start. Root advertises `catalog_s_g__memory_search` for PROJECT recall:

```json
{"text":"webhook replay horizon","top_k":5,"filter":{"exclude_mandatory":true},"ai_optimized":false}
```

`text` and `top_k` are required. Optional `mode` is `fts` (default, model-free), `semantic` or `hybrid`; semantic modes need the configured embedding service and fail explicitly instead of falling back. `filter` accepts `classification` (`fact`, `skill`, `tension`, `decision`, `convention`, `correction`), `tag`, `mandatory`, `important` and `exclude_mandatory`; `include_deleted_history` widens to historical content. Pass `project_dir`/`project_version` only to select another checkout or version; selectors grant no access. Discover a neighbor through `catalog_s_g__projects_list` when announced and use its authorized `checkouts[].dir`. A missing USER identity means USER Memory was not read, never that the personal store is empty.

Returned hits are evidence only to the extent of their supplied content. Compare a recalled decision with current AST and Knowledge evidence before relying on it: memories can go stale.

## What to remember

Memory exists so the project stops relearning the same things. Think of it in three kinds:

| Kind | What it holds | Where it goes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Episodic | Past requests, what was tried, outcomes and decisions taken in specific work | Task records it as you work (session description, checkpoints, comments of kind `decision`, `problem`, `lesson`). Promote a `decision` to Memory when it must be recalled outside that Task. |
| Semantic | Facts about the system, domain concepts, business rules, and the general preferences of the project and of the user | `fact` for verified behavior and business rules, `convention` for how the project wants things done (project preferences). Personal preferences of the user belong only in private USER memory. |
| Procedural | How to act: build, test, release and debugging recipes, workarounds, rules the agent must follow | `skill` for a reusable procedure, `correction` for a wrong approach and the right one; mark `mandatory` when every session must follow it. |
| Unresolved | Conflicting constraints and open trade-offs | `tension` |

## When to capture

Capture at the moment it happens; at the end of a long session the details and the reason are gone:
- The user corrects you, or says "always", "never", "prefer" or "don't" about the project → `correction` or `convention`.
- A decision is made or confirmed → `decision`, with the reason and the alternatives rejected.
- You discover something non-obvious: a root cause, hidden constraint, undocumented behavior, business rule or gotcha → `fact`.
- A procedure works after some trial (a command sequence, a debugging route, a workaround) → `skill`, with the exact steps.
- An approach fails for a reason future work would repeat → `correction`.
- Two valid constraints conflict and stay unresolved → `tension`.

Memory sweep: at every checkpoint, before a handoff, before closing a session and whenever the conversation grows long, ask what this work taught that the next session would otherwise rediscover, and capture each answer. A missed lesson costs more than an extra record: the Dream consolidation later merges duplicates, so when something is confirmed and plausibly reusable, save it. Skip only what the code, Git history or maintained documentation already state, transient progress, unconfirmed hypotheses and sensitive data.

## How to write from Root

Root has no Memory write, list or source tools; check the current catalogue before assuming otherwise. Note candidates as they arise (a Task comment of kind `lesson`, `decision` or `knowledge` keeps them safe), then at the sweep send one brief to the Scribe role listing every decided item: whether it updates an existing subject (with its ID) or is new, the title, a body with scope, rationale and provenance (Task, commit, page or source), the classification, tags, typed references, and whether it is mandatory or important. One subject per record; prefer updating an existing subject so its history survives. Never fabricate Role credentials or substitute the CLI for an unavailable MCP mutation.

Personal preferences of the user (language, response format, working style) have no agent write path: Role and Root Memory tools are PROJECT-only. Tell the engineer what you noticed and that `memory create --scope user` in the Graphit CLI stores it privately; do not put it in PROJECT Memory.

## Maintenance

`catalog_s_g__memory_index` ensures or, with `refresh: true`, rebuilds Memory lexical indexes and maintains embeddings when configured; `scope` selects `project` or `user`. Use it for an explicit administrative repair, not after writes. Periodic consolidation of duplicates and conflicts is done by the Dream process, not by ad hoc deletes.

When a task, session, memory or knowledge page relies on another record, explicitly send `references` with each target's `type` and `id`, plus `relation` (for example supports, implements, derived_from or relates_to). Resolve real IDs through the corresponding read tools; never invent them. Mentioning an ID in prose or making a Markdown link does not create a database relation. Send the complete intended explicit list on reference changes; omit it to preserve existing relations, and send [] to clear explicit relations. Structural task/session links remain managed by their existing fields. Qualify cross-project/user targets with `scope` and `scope_id`, and imported knowledge with `context`; use logical identities, never checkout paths.
Example write input: `references: [{"target": {"type": "memory", "id": "<verified memory ID>"}, "relation": "supports"}]`. The source is the record being written; do not repeat a source ID. Read its existing references before replacing the list so unrelated links survive.
Use `catalog_s_g__task_references` for outgoing/incoming Task or Session relations, and `catalog_s_g__knowledge_references` for outgoing document relations or incoming logical-target references in the admitted Knowledge corpus. Keep each origin PROJECT/version, target type/scope/context and independent direction cursor. A recorded foreign relation grants no target-content access. Use only operations advertised by the selected transport; report missing projection/repair capabilities instead of inventing a generic query or reconcile tool.

# Root contextual recall and decided persistence

Reuse standing context supplied by hooks. A question during implementation can need focused recall even without a new session, plan or blocker. Root offers PROJECT search; it does not announce the Role source/list/write tools or a USER search fallback.

## A question in the middle of work

When a replay horizon lacks a retained explanation, call the advertised `catalog_s_g__memory_search` using the current project's resolved checkout only in the live envelope:

```json
{"text":"webhook replay horizon","filter":{"exclude_mandatory":true},"top_k":5,"ai_optimized":false}
```

Read the actual supplied hit content. Titles alone do not establish conditions or provenance. If full retrieval is needed, route the exact returned ID to an authorized Role announcing `catalog_s_g__memory_source`; do not invent a Root source call. A referenced Task ID can be read through `catalog_s_g__task_get` under that tool's actual envelope and authority, without claiming or reopening historical work. Compare the recorded conditions with current AST/Knowledge evidence; a memory that contradicts current code is a finding to report, not a rule to follow blindly.

## Is it worth saving?

Save it when all of these hold: it is confirmed (by the user, a decision record, a test or the source), it will matter to future work beyond the current Task, and it is not already obvious from the code, Git history or maintained documentation. # Graphit Task

Task is the durable record of a demand: what was asked (the Session), how it will be delivered (Tasks with typed checks), what happened (progress, checkpoints, comments and check evidence) and which commit delivered it. It exists so that any agent can resume after interruption, compaction or handoff from the records alone, so write every description and checkpoint for a reader who never saw this conversation.

Roles: the coordinator owns Task claims, acceptance, checkpoints and lifecycle. A delegated role reads the session and Task IDs it was given, reports anchored findings, and returns a draft for any write that needs a claim; it never creates, claims, revises, completes, cancels or releases coordination state. Use the authenticated MCP catalogue; never edit Task tables or substitute another server or a CLI for a missing operation.

Persistence boundary for every module: shared project records hold only non-sensitive content the project needs (contracts, decisions, evidence, operations). Never persist personal or sensitive user/organization data, secrets, credentials, security-risk material, feelings or unconfirmed speculation. A durable, useful personal preference or correction belongs only in private user memory. Label technical hypotheses as hypotheses.

## Workflow

1. Recover: find the session for this demand and read its latest checkpoint and linked Tasks. Read [references/session.md](references/session.md) before starting, resuming or handing off coordination.
2. Decide: continue the same evolving demand in its session, revise it when scope changed, and create a new session only for a different demand. The host chat ID is not a Task Session ID.
3. Specify: investigate through AST, Knowledge, Memory and Task, then save the plan as dependency-ordered Tasks with acceptance and test checks. Read [references/planning.md](references/planning.md) for a multi-outcome plan, [references/worked-feature.md](references/worked-feature.md) for one filled feature and [references/worked-system.md](references/worked-system.md) for several deliveries.
4. Execute: claim a ready leaf, implement, record check evidence and progress. Read [references/execution.md](references/execution.md) before a leaf, review or handoff.
5. Checkpoint: at each meaningful outcome, checkpoint the Session with evidence, decisions and the exact next step.
6. Close: complete Tasks whose checks passed, associate the delivered commit, and complete the Session once every linked Task is terminal; cancel explicitly when the demand is withdrawn.

Claim nothing merely to read or wait, and reuse context you already recovered.

## Tool map

Use only operations advertised by the current server, and read a tool's input schema before its first use; a name on another server does not establish this server's API.

| Need | Tool |
| --- | --- |
| Find or read a session | `catalog_s_g__task_session_list`, `catalog_s_g__task_session_get` |

## Wire contract

Native Task calls use an optional `selection` and, when the operation needs it, an `input` object; domain fields belong inside them. The optional strict boolean `ai_optimized` belongs at the argument root: omitted/`true` returns TOON text, without duplicate JSON `structuredContent`; `false` returns JSON for machine consumers. There is no caller-selected `agent_id`; the authenticated caller is the actor.

Selection DATA identifies an already retained PROJECT/version; it grants no access. Prefer captured `selection.project_id` and `selection.project_version`. A directory selector is `selection.project_dir`, one Unicode path string; echo the captured path exactly. Read the returned record after each mutation and use its current revision; never guess an increment.

Known IDs: `catalog_s_g__task_get` or `catalog_s_g__task_session_get` with only `input.id` return the current record, `creation`, `last_event`, `generation` and start cursors; `history` and `comments` stay null (unloaded). Request history with `input.history={page_size,cursor}` (Task also `input.comments`), starting from the returned start cursor and continuing with `next_cursor`. A loaded empty list differs from an unloaded null section. Request only the pages that answer the question; a complete audit traverses through EOF at the same pin.

Discovery: `catalog_s_g__task_search` searches current Task specifications, retained check evidence and comments with `input.text`, `input.filter`, positive `input.page_size` and `input.top_k`; optional `input.mode` is `fts` (model-free default), `semantic` or `hybrid` when the schema offers it. Continue any cursor with unchanged selection and parameters. A `no_corpus` state differs from a published empty result. Cursors are DATA, never authority.

Recall prior investigations, decisions and evidence whenever a new doubt arises during the work, not only at the start; stop once the gap is closed.

## References and commits

When a task, session, memory or knowledge page relies on another record, explicitly send `references` with each target's `type` and `id`, plus `relation` (for example supports, implements, derived_from or relates_to). Resolve real IDs through the corresponding read tools; never invent them. Mentioning an ID in prose or making a Markdown link does not create a database relation. Send the complete intended explicit list on reference changes; omit it to preserve existing relations, and send [] to clear explicit relations. Structural task/session links remain managed by their existing fields. Qualify cross-project/user targets with `scope` and `scope_id`, and imported knowledge with `context`; use logical identities, never checkout paths.
Example write input: `references: [{"target": {"type": "memory", "id": "<verified memory ID>"}, "relation": "supports"}]`. The source is the record being written; do not repeat a source ID. Read its existing references before replacing the list so unrelated links survive.
Use `catalog_s_g__task_references` for outgoing/incoming Task or Session relations, and `catalog_s_g__knowledge_references` for outgoing document relations or incoming logical-target references in the admitted Knowledge corpus. Keep each origin PROJECT/version, target type/scope/context and independent direction cursor. A recorded foreign relation grants no target-content access. Use only operations advertised by the selected transport; report missing projection/repair capabilities instead of inventing a generic query or reconcile tool.


Creation, comments and supported owner mutations expose `input.references`: omitted preserves authored relations, `[]` clears them, and a complete array replaces them. Each entry requires `target:{type,id}` and `relation`; optional `field`, `target.scope`, `target.scope_id` and `target.context` are strings. Claims and heartbeats have no reference patch.

After an authorized Git commit or amend succeeds, resolve the full commit ID (`git rev-parse HEAD`) and update `Task.commit` on the Tasks whose changes are actually included using `catalog_s_g__task_commit_set`. This also applies to completed Tasks; preserve their status and check evidence. Never infer a commit from a planned command or treat this instruction as authorization to commit or push.

For an explicitly withdrawn demand, resolve linked Tasks individually before calling `catalog_s_g__task_session_cancel` with the current revision, reason and live coordinator claim when owned. Do not complete a cancelled demand or silently cascade cancellation. A terminal retry must omit claim and references.

# Specify executable work before implementation

This reference describes coordinator-owned workflows. A delegated role reads the IDs it was given, reports anchored findings and returns a draft for any write that needs a claim.

The coordinator owns acceptance, checks, checkpoints and lifecycle. Read [session.md](session.md) for the evolving demand. This is an authoring model for descriptions and native typed checks, not extra MCP fields. Use the user's language and existing project terminology; omit irrelevant sections rather than writing placeholder boilerplate.

## Establish evidence and intent

Capture purpose, actors/consumers, journeys, supplied examples, boundaries, constraints and observable finish. Inventory distinct requirements before compressing a large request. A small fix can be one packet; a feature needs independently demonstrable slices; a system needs deliveries and their shared contracts.

Separate verified facts (source/version/observation), supported assumptions (basis, effect if false and validation) and open decisions (exact question, affected requirement, resolver and blocked action). Read current implementation through AST, maintained contracts through Knowledge, durable decisions through Memory/Task, and ecosystem identity through the supported Hub route.

Resolve material authority, data retention, provider, destructive-effect and compatibility decisions before dependent work. Do not invent them to make a packet ready: write the open question explicitly in the description (for example prefixed `NEEDS CLARIFICATION:`) and keep the affected leaf unclaimed until it is answered. Preserve accepted answers and reconcile contradictions with rationale.

## Specify contracts and proof

Give journeys/requirements stable prose labels. State starting condition, action, result and priority rationale. Cover alternate/empty/error/denied/recovery states when applicable. Describe real data types, identities/ownership, required/optional values, omitted/null/empty distinctions, lifetimes, state transitions, effects, idempotency, concurrency and errors. Selectors/metadata are never grants.

Use observable obligations, not 'fast/secure/works'. A useful acceptance check reads as a testable condition, for example "when the include flag is false, the list returns only active rows and the same total as today". Include performance, accessibility, availability, resource or other constraints only when requested or verified; do not invent targets, quotas or capacity campaigns. Distinguish release proof from outcomes requiring later production observation.

The technical plan names current components, public APIs and boundaries, exact file/interface ownership, settled choices and alternatives where material, prerequisites and useful slices. Missing contracts are refinement prerequisites, not mocks, Boolean authority callbacks or untested assumptions.

For each unit define a meaningful fixture/setup, action/command and expected result, plus the affected source/docs and evidence owner. Reuse mature APIs and existing tests. Each code/config/behavior unit checks its maintained docs; each documentation unit checks real implementation. Choose proportionate fast and long gates; an ad hoc success is not a proven installed regression barrier. Never initiate a push merely to exercise its guard.

## Save the graph

Group by outcome and accountable ownership, not tool-call/file count. Create prerequisite/parent records before their returned IDs are used. Native creation supplies session_id, title, description, task_type, priority and `checks` with acceptance/test kinds; parent_id/depends_on and explicit calendar schedule follow the actual schema.
